notes: Batch 1 (40 species), prepared by the coding agent on 2026-11-21 at the owner's request, for a portfolio project. Sources read that day: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy (CC BY 4.0) and GBIF species profiles (WoRMS flags) via the GBIF API; Wikidata (CC0) for the IUCN category, cited second-hand with the IUCN edition its statement references; English Wikipedia (revision ids recorded) for population figures, cited second-hand. IUCN pages were not read (robots.txt disallows this agent). Images from Wikimedia Commons: licence read from Commons metadata and compared with the file's embedded copyright fields; files without a named creator were not used. Trend is 'unknown' throughout (not stated by Wikidata). Countries and regions are not set.

editorial.overview: The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) is a mammal of the family Ursidae, in the order Carnivora. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Almost entirely bamboo, which can make up about 99% of what it eats; a panda may eat up to 38 kg in a day. Its gut is still that of a carnivore, so it needs a lot of bamboo, and it needs more than one bamboo species in case one flowers and dies back.

populationEstimates.method: Wild pandas older than 1.5 years, excluding dependent young (Fourth National Survey, China, 2011–2014, published 2015)

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: WWF's figure; no survey year given on the page.

editorial.overview: The tiger (Panthera tigris) is a mammal of the family Felidae, in the order Carnivora. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An apex predator that hunts mainly large hoofed animals such as deer and wild boar; in India it also takes water buffalo, bison and antelope.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Roughly 4,500 wild tigers in the 2022 IUCN assessment, up from about 3,200 in 2015, as reported by Panthera. Another source gives 3,726 to 5,578 excluding cubs.

editorial.overview: The african bush elephant (Loxodonta africana) is a mammal of the family Elephantidae, in the order Proboscidea. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A plant eater. It strips leaves and branches from trees and bushes with its trunk, and can eat up to about 136 kg of food and drink 113 to 190 litres of water in a day.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Bush elephants only. One source gives about 265,000 (the 415,000 total for all African elephants minus about 150,000 forest elephants), another a rounded 300,000. Approximate.

editorial.overview: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is a mammal of the family Hominidae, in the order Primates. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly plants. Mountain gorillas eat leaves, shoots, stems, wild celery and bamboo, and occasionally insects. Grauer's gorillas eat a wider mix including fruit.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as "less than 6,000" by 2016.
Our sum of two figures: about 1,004 mountain gorillas plus 3,800 (2015) to 6,800 (2021) Grauer's gorillas. Both subspecies are counted; the figures come from different years.

editorial.overview: The bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) is a mammal of the family Hominidae, in the order Primates. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly fruit, around 60% of its diet, with wild figs and durians favoured. It also eats leaves, shoots, insects and bark.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 104,000 Bornean orangutans per WWF. A 2018 study put the remaining total between 70,000 and about 100,000.

editorial.overview: The red Panda (Ailurus fulgens) is a mammal of the family Ailuridae, in the order Carnivora. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly bamboo, about 98% of its diet. It occasionally eats acorns, fruit, roots, eggs, small rodents and small birds.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as an estimate of 10,000 individuals; no year given.
No exact count exists. The high end is a 2015 estimate of about 10,000; the low end is China's lower regional estimate (3,000 to 7,000) alone. India is estimated separately at 5,000 to 6,000.

editorial.overview: The blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus) is a mammal of the family Balaenopteridae, in the order Cetacea. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly krill, up to about 6 tonnes a day for the biggest animals. It occasionally takes small fish and copepods.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: From The Canadian Encyclopedia. Another summary lists 400 to 1,400 in the Southern Ocean alone, so the global total is approximate.

editorial.overview: The polar bear (Ursus maritimus) is a mammal of the family Ursidae, in the order Carnivora. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Hunts mostly seals from the sea ice, especially ringed seals; in late spring and early summer it gets about two thirds of its yearly energy this way.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Attributed by the article to the IUCN; no year given.

editorial.overview: The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is a mammal of the family Felidae, in the order Carnivora. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small to medium antelope such as gazelle and impala, plus birds and small mammals; sometimes young wildebeest. Where wild prey is scarce it may take livestock.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Estimate for 2021.

editorial.overview: The black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis) is a mammal of the family Rhinocerotidae, in the order Perissodactyla. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A browser. It plucks leaves and twigs from acacia and other woody plants with its pointed upper lip; grass is a minor part. About 200 plant species have been recorded.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Attributed by the article to the IUCN; no year given.

editorial.overview: The vaquita (Phocoena sinus) is a mammal of the family Phocoenidae, in the order Cetacea. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small fish, shrimp and other crustaceans, and squid and octopus. Stomach contents show it is not picky: it eats whatever is plentiful, mostly bottom-dwelling fish such as grunts and croakers. Sources disagree on whether prey is near the surface or near the bottom.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as "fewer than 19" remaining in the wild in 2018.

editorial.overview: The koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) is a mammal of the family Phascolarctidae, in the order Diprotodontia. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Leaves, almost all of them from eucalypt trees (about 70 eucalypt species and 30 others are eaten). The leaves also supply most of its water.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: A very wide range: some experts say as few as 60,000, a popular-science source up to about 520,000. Official national counts are inconsistent.

editorial.overview: The california condor (Gymnogyps californianus) is a bird of the family Cathartidae, in the order Accipitriformes. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A scavenger. It eats mostly the carcasses of large mammals and sometimes small mammals such as ground squirrels.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild birds: about 347 as of 2022 (a later summary; plus about 214 in captivity), and 290 in an older Audubon listing. Counts depend on the year.

editorial.overview: The philippine Eagle (Pithecophaga jefferyi) is a bird of the family Accipitridae, in the order Accipitriformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as terrestrial. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly mammals such as civets and colugos, along with birds, snakes, monitor lizards, bats and monkeys; prey varies by island.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Mindanao only, where the largest numbers live; no year given.

editorial.overview: The whooping crane (Grus americana) is a bird of the family Gruidae, in the order Gruiformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as terrestrial. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore. In the breeding season it eats mostly small fish and water invertebrates; in winter, blue crabs, clams and wolfberry; on migration, waste grain in fields.

populationEstimates.qualitativeText: About 560 in the migratory Aransas–Wood Buffalo population and about 140 in two reintroduced populations (Wisconsin and Louisiana), as of 2025

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as "about 130".

editorial.overview: The emperor Penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) is a bird of the family Spheniscidae, in the order Sphenisciformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine and terrestrial. It is listed as Near threatened on the IUCN Red List, as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly fish, with squid and krill. In one study fish were about 78% of the diet by mass, often Antarctic silverfish. Squid and krill matter more at some sites and seasons, and parents change what they hunt when rearing chicks.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: About 256,500 breeding pairs in 54 colonies per BirdLife. Other counts: 238,000 pairs (Pew, 2014) and over 275,000 (Britannica).

editorial.overview: The snowy Owl (Bubo scandiacus) is a bird of the family Strigidae, in the order Strigiformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as terrestrial. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly lemmings, which can be up to 95% of the diet in the breeding season. Outside it, also other rodents, hares, rabbits, seabirds, ducks and geese.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Stated as "probably fewer than 100,000", from 2010s–2020s data.
Stated as "28,000 or even considerably less" successful breeding pairs.

editorial.overview: The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is a bird of the family Accipitridae, in the order Accipitriformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine and freshwater and terrestrial. It is listed as Least concern on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly fish (about 56% of prey at active nests), plus birds (28%) and mammals (14%). Also waterfowl, small mammals and carrion.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: A 2021 US Fish and Wildlife Service estimate for the lower 48 states (including 71,467 breeding pairs in 2018-2019). Alaska and Canada are not included.

editorial.overview: The atlantic Puffin (Fratercula arctica) is a bird of the family Alcidae, in the order Charadriiformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine and terrestrial. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Almost entirely fish; occasionally shrimp, other crustaceans, molluscs and marine worms.

populationEstimates.qualitativeText: In Europe, which holds more than 90% of the global population: 4,770,000–5,780,000 pairs (9,550,000–11,600,000 adults)

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: BirdLife's global estimate, rated poor quality and dated 2011.

editorial.overview: The komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) is a reptile of the family Varanidae. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly carrion; adults also take large prey such as deer, wild boar and water buffalo. Young dragons are sometimes eaten by adults.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Assessed as 3,222 in 2013 and 3,092 in 2014.

editorial.overview: The leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) is a reptile of the family Dermochelyidae. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Almost only jellyfish and other soft-bodied animals; it also eats some seaweed, fish and crustaceans. It can die from swallowing plastic mistaken for jellyfish.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Nesting females only, not all adults. Sources give 34,000 to 36,000 (about 35,860 in one). Pacific populations have fallen far more than Atlantic ones.

editorial.overview: The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is a reptile of the family Gavialidae. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as freshwater and terrestrial. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults eat almost only fish. Juveniles also take insects, crustaceans and frogs.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Roughly 200 mature wild gharials per San Diego Zoo; another source says about 182 individuals.

editorial.overview: The green turtle (Chelonia mydas) is a reptile of the family Cheloniidae. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Least concern on the IUCN Red List (2025.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults mostly eat seagrass and algae, the only sea turtle that is mainly a plant eater.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Nesting females only, not all adults; the source gives no date.

editorial.overview: The tuatara (Sphenodon punctatus) is a reptile of the family Sphenodontidae. It is listed as Least concern on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mostly invertebrates, about 75% of the diet, especially beetles, grasshoppers and wetas; sometimes lizards and small birds.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Approximate. The largest single population, on Stephens Island, is at least 30,000.

editorial.overview: The golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) is a amphibian of the family Dendrobatidae, in the order Anura. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Insects, other small arthropods and worms. Its poison seems to come from its prey: frogs raised in captivity without these insects are not poisonous.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No total count. It is abundant within its very small range (under 5,000 square km) in western Colombia, and the trend is decreasing.

editorial.overview: The chinese giant salamander (Andrias davidianus) is a amphibian of the family Cryptobranchidae, in the order Caudata. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as freshwater. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: The sources we read gave little detail. They note it is strongly cannibalistic, with about 27% of the diet by weight being its own species.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: Unknown, but the wild population is reported to have fallen by more than 80% since the 1950s and is nearly extinct in the wild in places.

editorial.overview: The hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis) is a amphibian of the family Cryptobranchidae, in the order Caudata. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as freshwater. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Mainly crayfish in warm months, with more fish in winter; young ones also eat worms and insects.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: Of 626 known historical populations, about 41% are thought to be extirpated and another 36% are declining. No total count of animals.

editorial.overview: The lemur Leaf Frog (Agalychnis lemur) is a amphibian of the family Phyllomedusidae, in the order Anura. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Small insects and other invertebrates such as flies, ants and moths, according to zoo sources. Its wild diet has not been formally reported.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No count. Once common in Costa Rica, it has declined sharply over about two decades and survives at only a few sites there.

editorial.overview: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is a fish of the family Rhincodontidae, in the order Orectolobiformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: A filter feeder that eats mostly plankton and small fish.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No global count exists. The Indo-Pacific population is thought to have fallen about 63% over 75 years and the Atlantic population by more than 30%.

editorial.overview: The great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) is a fish of the family Lamnidae, in the order Lamniformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults mainly eat seals, sea lions, dolphins and whale carcasses; the diet also includes fish, other sharks, turtles and seabirds.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No global count exists. One conservation group says fewer than 3,500 worldwide, but another study counted about 5,460 in eastern Australasia alone, so the two disagree. The northeast Pacific population seems to be increasing.

editorial.overview: The beluga (Huso huso) is a fish of the family Acipenseridae, in the order Acipenseriformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine and freshwater. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Young fish eat invertebrates; from about 10 cm long they switch to fish. Adults eat mostly large fish, in the Caspian chiefly roach, herring and gobies.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No current count found. It is critically endangered, and its low resilience means a population needs more than 14 years to double.

editorial.overview: The atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) is a fish of the family Scombridae, in the order Perciformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Least concern on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults mostly eat smaller fish, crustaceans, squid and eels; the diet can also include jellyfish and octopus.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No single population count is published. The western stock is not currently subject to overfishing, but whether it is overfished is unknown; an advocacy group reports falls of at least 60% (east) and 82% (west) since the 1970s.

editorial.overview: The scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini) is a fish of the family Sphyrnidae, in the order Carcharhiniformes. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Opportunistic: it eats whatever is plentiful, from small fish and squid to crustaceans, other sharks and rays.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No global count exists. Declines of 50% to 90% have been reported in parts of its range, and one source says more than 80% overall.

editorial.overview: The monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus) is a insect of the family Nymphalidae, in the order Lepidoptera. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as terrestrial. It is listed as Least concern on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Caterpillars eat milkweed leaves, the plant they depend on. Adult feeding was not covered in the sources we read.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: Counted by the area of forest the butterflies cover in Mexico each winter, not by individuals. The eastern population has fallen since counts began in 1993, and the western population has also declined.

editorial.overview: The rusty patched bumble bee (Bombus affinis) is a insect of the family Apidae, in the order Hymenoptera. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Pollen and nectar from a wide range of flowering plants.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No total count. Abundance is reported down about 87%, and since 2000 it has been seen in only 13 US states and one Canadian province, against 28 states and two provinces before.

editorial.overview: The lord Howe Island stick insect (Dryococelus australis) is a insect of the family Phasmatidae, in the order Phasmida. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Adults feed at night on the leaf tips of the tea tree shrubs where they live, and hide by day.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Wild animals on Ball's Pyramid, the only wild site. Another zoo page says 20 to 30.

editorial.overview: The giant clam (Tridacna gigas) is a mollusc of the family Cardiidae, in the order Cardiida. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Gets most of its nutrition from algae living in its tissues (up to 90% of its carbon) and also filters plankton from the water.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No global count. Wild numbers are described as greatly reduced by harvesting, and recovery is slow (population doubling takes about 4.5 to 14 years).

editorial.overview: The elkhorn coral (Acropora palmata) is a coral of the family Acroporidae, in the order Scleractinia. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Gets energy mainly from the algae living in it, and can catch small fish and zooplankton with its tentacles.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: Now about 3% or less of its former abundance across the Caribbean, after a disease event in the 1980s.

editorial.overview: The coconut crab (Birgus latro) is a crustacean of the family Coenobitidae, in the order Decapoda. The World Register of Marine Species, as listed by GBIF, records it as marine and terrestrial. It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (2022.2 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: An omnivore that eats plants and animals, including coconut, pandanus and other palm fruit.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: No published count found; described in words from the source.
populationEstimates.qualitativeText: No global count. Populations have fallen or disappeared across much of its range through hunting and habitat loss.

editorial.overview: The kakapo (Strigops habroptila) is a bird of the family Psittacidae, in the order Psittaciformes. It is listed as Critically endangered on the IUCN Red List (2021.3 edition), as recorded on Wikidata.

diet.narrative: Entirely plants: leaves, buds, flowers, fern fronds, bark, roots, fruit and seeds.

populationEstimates.uncertaintyNote: Total known population of living individuals, as of 2026. Every bird is individually known.
235 birds alive per the Department of Conservation page; another DOC report says almost 250.
